title: Nigerian Pidgin
motto: The most expressive, energetic lingua franca across West Africa!
description: Learn the vibrant language spoken by over 75 million people across Nigeria, West Africa, and global Afrobeat culture — structured with the NERDC 4-Tier Oracy, Grammar, and Literature framework.

proverbOfDay.proverb: Monkey dey work, baboon dey chop.
proverbOfDay.translation: One person toils while another unjustly enjoys the fruit of the labor.
proverbOfDay.context: The master proverb of Nigerian civic and commercial discourse, addressing unfair compensation, uncredited teamwork, and the struggle for equity.

cultureTips.title: The Sacred Greeting: 'How You Dey?' & Tone Variations
cultureTips.description: When meeting anyone in Nigeria, a cheerful 'How you dey?' or 'How far?' breaks all social friction. The reply can vary from 'I dey fine' (standard), to 'We dey push am' (humble resilience), or 'I dey kampe' (unshakeable energy).

cultureTips.title: The Danfo Transit Etiquette & 'Owa o!'
cultureTips.description: In the famous yellow Danfo buses across Lagos, passengers must always alert the conductor before their stop by loudly calling 'Owa o!' (meaning 'Someone is alighting here!'). Always carry 'change' (small denomination notes) to avoid conductor disputes.

cultureTips.title: Food Hospitality: The Compulsory 'Come and Chop!'
cultureTips.description: Whenever you are eating in the presence of colleagues, guests, or neighbors, it is cultural etiquette to warmly invite them: 'Come and chop!' A polite refusal is simply: 'Thank you, I dey alright' or 'Enjoy your food.'

cultureTips.title: The Magic Softener: 'Abeg'
cultureTips.description: 'Abeg' literally translates to 'I beg you' (Please). Placing 'Abeg' at the beginning or end of a question instantly diffuses tension, conveys mutual respect, and turns any hard negotiation into a warm transaction.

cultureTips.title: The Art of Market Haggling: 'How Much Last?'
cultureTips.description: In open-air markets (like Balogun, Ariaria, or Bodija), the quoted initial price is never final. The buyer begins by asking 'How much last, my sister?' Building rapport, laughing together, and calling the seller 'Customer' or 'Oga/Madam' guarantees the best price.

cultureTips.title: Respect for Elders: 'Bros', 'Uncle', and 'Ma'
cultureTips.description: Never call an elder or senior acquaintance by their bare first name in NPE. Prefixing with 'Bros' (for older peers), 'Uncle/Aunty' (for generationally older contacts), or 'Sir/Ma' reflects the deep communal respect foundational to Nigerian culture.

customUnits.title: Unit 1: Phonology & Sound Substitutions
customUnits.subtitle: Foundational phonetic shifts: dental fricative substitution (/θ/ and /ð/ to /t/ and /d/), initial /h/ dropping, and pronoun grid.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Dental Fricative Shift & Initial H Dropping
lessons.description: Master standard consonant sound substitutions (thing -> ting, them -> dem) and the dropping of initial 'h' (house -> ouse).

questions.prompt: In Nigerian Pidgin phonology, how is the English voiceless dental fricative 'th' in 'thing' pronounced?
options: It remains identical to British English 'thing'
questions.explanation: Nigerian Pidgin (West Africa) systematically replaces the voiceless dental fricative /θ/ with the alveolar plosive /t/ (thing -> ting, thank -> tank, three -> tree).

questions.prompt: How does the voiced 'th' in 'them' or 'they' sound in standard Nigerian Pidgin?
questions.explanation: The voiced dental fricative /ð/ systematically becomes /d/, producing 'dem' (them/they), 'dat' (that), and 'dis' (this).

questions.prompt: What happens to the initial 'h' sound in words like 'house' or 'hospital' in everyday Pidgin speech?
options: The /h/ is intensified into a harsh guttural sound
An extra 'k' is added before the /h/
It is always pronounced with British RP precision
questions.explanation: NPE phonotactics frequently drops initial voiceless glottal fricatives /h/, yielding 'ouse' for house, 'ospital' for hospital, and 'ungry' for hungry.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: 'I want go back to my _____ (house).'
questions.sentence: I want go back to my ___ (house).
questions.explanation: With the initial /h/ dropped, 'house' is rendered as 'ouse'.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Vowel Systems & Orthographic Precision
lessons.description: Understand the 7-vowel system of Nigerian Pidgin, vowel harmony, and standard written spellings (chop, wetin, commot, sabi).

questions.prompt: How many vowel phonemes characterize the core Nigerian Pidgin sound system?
options: 7 vowels (/i, e, ɛ, a, ɔ, o, u/)
5 vowels only (/a, e, i, o, u/)
12 pure vowels like British Received Pronunciation
questions.correctAnswer: 7 vowels (/i, e, ɛ, a, ɔ, o, u/)
questions.explanation: Unlike English with 12 monopthongs, NPE uses a 7-vowel African substrate system including open /ɛ/ and open /ɔ/.

questions.prompt: What does the high-frequency verb 'chop' mean in Nigerian Pidgin?
options: To cut wood with an axe only
questions.explanation: 'Chop' is the foundational verb meaning to eat, dine, or enjoy consumption.

questions.prompt: What is the meaning of the essential question word 'wetin'?
questions.explanation: 'Wetin' is derived from 'what thing' and is the universal question word for 'what' (e.g. 'Wetin dey happen?').

questions.prompt: What does the Portuguese-derived word 'sabi' mean?
options: To know / to understand / to be skilled
questions.correctAnswer: To know / to understand / to be skilled
questions.explanation: 'Sabi' comes from Portuguese 'saber' and means to know or possess competence.
